questions.stem_markdown: During a routine adolescent review, a parent says, "My 15-year-old can explain why risky dares are dangerous, but still does reckless things with friends." Which explanation best matches the note-based model of adolescent risk-taking?

options.text: Adolescents generally cannot think abstractly until adulthood
Reward-oriented and emotionally arousing systems intensify before the prefrontal cortex fully matures
Risk-taking in adolescence usually means severe intellectual disability
The adolescent brain is structurally stable after childhood
Risk-taking is mainly caused by a lack of school discipline

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes describe adolescence as a period of neuronal overgrowth and pruning, with the prefrontal cortex maturing last. This helps explain why reward orientation and emotional arousal can outpace regulatory control, especially during the years when risk-taking is prominent.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes state that abstract thought develops during adolescence rather than appearing only in adulthood.
why_others_wrong.C: The source material does not equate typical adolescent risk-taking with intellectual disability.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes specifically describe major brain development during adolescence, not structural stability.
why_others_wrong.E: School context matters, but the note-based explanation for risk-taking is neurodevelopmental rather than purely disciplinary.

key_takeaways: Adolescence involves major brain remodelling.
The prefrontal cortex matures later than systems linked to reward and arousal.
Risk-taking can persist even when an adolescent can describe possible consequences.

A low-resilience profile should trigger active follow-up rather than reassurance alone.
